---
title: Tailwind CSS v4
description: Using okcolor alongside Tailwind CSS v4's built-in OKLCH utilities.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

Tailwind CSS v4 ships with OKLCH-based colors. okcolor works alongside it — it leaves Tailwind's own OKLCH utilities untouched and only transforms legacy colors in your custom CSS.

## What gets left alone

Tailwind's built-in colors are already OKLCH:

```css
/* These are generated by Tailwind — okcolor ignores them */
.bg-blue-500      /* uses oklch internally */
.text-red-600     /* uses oklch internally */
.shadow-lg        /* uses oklch internally */
```

## What gets converted

Your custom CSS with legacy color formats:

```css
/* Input: your custom CSS */
.my-brand {
  color: #1a1a2e;
  background: hsl(250, 80%, 60%);
  border-color: rgb(26 26 46);
}
```

```css
/* Output: all legacy colors become oklch */
.my-brand {
  color: oklch(17.68% 0.06562 274.54);
  background: oklch(53.8% 0.22014 268.54);
  border-color: oklch(17.68% 0.06562 274.54);
}
```

## Configuration

In your `vite.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite'
import { okColor } from 'okcolor'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    tailwindcss(),
    okColor(),
  ],
})
```

Plugin order does not matter for correctness. Vite handles the CSS pipeline stages correctly regardless of declaration order.

## Why migrate to OKLCH?

If you're designing with OKLCH values, your color scales are perceptually uniform:

```css
/* Perceptually uniform scale (constant hue, linear lightness steps) */
:root {
  --brand-100: oklch(0.95 0.02 250);
  --brand-200: oklch(0.85 0.04 250);
  --brand-300: oklch(0.75 0.08 250);
  --brand-400: oklch(0.65 0.12 250);
  --brand-500: oklch(0.55 0.16 250);
  --brand-600: oklch(0.45 0.14 250);
  --brand-700: oklch(0.35 0.10 250);
  --brand-800: oklch(0.25 0.06 250);
  --brand-900: oklch(0.15 0.03 250);
}
```

Compare this with HSL, where equal lightness steps produce wildly different perceived brightness:

```css
/* HSL: same 'lightness' but very different perceived brightness */
color: hsl(250, 80%, 50%);   /* purple — looks dark */
color: hsl(120, 80%, 50%);   /* green  — looks bright */
color: hsl(60, 80%, 50%);    /* yellow — looks extremely bright */
```

With okcolor, you can keep writing legacy formats and let the engine handle the conversion. Or write OKLCH directly and enjoy perceptual uniformity from the start.
